topline: Four stories today: Poland's fight over its constitutional court turns into a street-level stand-off, Brussels tables the last €45bn of Ukraine's loan for 2027, Canada and the EU pledge an 'ever closer association' after the associate-member label is dropped, and a new €2 EU fee on cheap non-EU parcels starts on Sunday.

stories.title: Poland's constitutional court chief suspended as riot police guard the tribunal and the president flies home
stories.summary: On Friday a judge elected by parliament but never sworn in by President Karol Nawrocki announced the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, and seven newly elected judges entered the court building escorted by state protection officers. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for both men's immunity to be lifted, while the tribunal's own account called the move a coup d'état and said the judge who signed the order was not a member of the court. Nawrocki turned his plane back from a state visit to Senegal, riot police were deployed outside the tribunal, and police said protesters from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) camp threw objects at officers. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said restoring the rule of law was the government's duty, even if the process is painful; PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński said Poland had become a police state.
stories.why: The tribunal, filled with PiS appointees between 2015 and 2023, was at the heart of Poland's long rule-of-law clash with Brussels and once ruled that Polish law outranks EU law. How Warsaw unpicks that legacy, and whether the method itself is lawful, is now a test case for the whole EU.

left.angle: Centre-left and lean-left coverage frames the day as an institutional crisis rooted in the PiS era's capture of the court. It tends to attribute the word 'coup' to the opposition or the tribunal rather than using it, and gives more room to the background: unrecognised judges, rulings the government ignores, and a European Court of Human Rights order to seat the new judges.

outlets.name: El País
outlets.note: Presents the suspension as setting off an institutional crisis; does not adopt the 'coup' label.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Arabic-language report that explicitly attributes the 'coup' description to the opposition.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage leads with the drama: riot police at a court, a president turning his plane around, and the 'coup' charge made by the tribunal and PiS figures. It amplifies opposition voices such as Zbigniew Ziobro and, in the UK, Nigel Farage, while the government's legal case gets comparatively little space; the more measured pieces still note PiS's own record of fines from Brussels.

outlets.name: GB News
outlets.note: Headlines the court's 'coup d'état' claim and Nigel Farage calling the protests very serious.

outlets.name: Fox News
outlets.note: Puts 'coup' in the headline; quotes Ziobro urging resistance and Morawiecki on a 'forceful takeover', with Tusk's one-line defence.

stories.differ: The left asks whether the government's method fixes a captured court; the right asks whether the government just seized one. The same events are labelled an 'institutional crisis' on one side and a 'coup' on the other.

stories.title: Commission proposes final €45bn of Ukraine's EU loan for 2027 as a wider funding gap looms
stories.summary: The European Commission on Friday proposed releasing the second half of the €90bn Ukraine Support Loan: €45bn for 2027, of which up to €31.7bn would go to Ukraine's defence industry and up to €13.3bn to budget support. The proposal follows a positive assessment of Kyiv's 2027 financing strategy and now needs Council approval, with payments expected early next year. Of this year's €45bn, €19.8bn has been paid out so far, and budget support stays tied to rule-of-law and anti-corruption conditions. Ursula von der Leyen said the money gives Ukraine predictability; the EU's total support since 2022 now stands at €231.6bn. Even so, Ukraine's needs for 2027 exceed what the loan covers by roughly €70bn, which Brussels wants allies such as the UK, Canada and Japan to help fill.
stories.why: With US support uncertain, EU money is now the backbone of Ukraine's state budget and arms purchases. How the remaining 2027 gap is filled, through partners, more joint debt or Russian assets, is due to come up at the EU leaders' summit in late November.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage treats the loan as necessary but insufficient, and frames the real story as burden-sharing: Europe already provides most external aid, so the UK, Canada, Japan and others are being pushed to step up. It relies heavily on EU officials and Kyiv's own figures. This is earlier coverage of the funding gap; we did not find a fresh left-leaning take on Friday's proposal itself.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Earlier (21 Oct): EU looks to allies to plug a €70bn hole for 2027, stressing Europe already carries 80% of external aid.

right.angle: We found no right-leaning take on Friday's €45bn proposal. Earlier conservative coverage of the €90bn loan focused on the politics around it, especially Hungary's past blocking and the new government in Budapest, and on joint EU borrowing rather than on Ukraine's needs.

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Earlier (23 Apr): covered the loan's unblocking after Orbán's exit, with scepticism over Ukraine's pipeline claims.

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets ask how Europe can get others to pay a fair share; conservative outlets have mostly asked what the borrowing costs Europe and who decided it, though neither side had much to say about Friday's proposal itself.

stories.title: EU and Canada pledge 'ever closer association' after Germany blocks the associate-member label
stories.summary: At their summit in Montreal on Friday, the EU and Canada agreed to widen cooperation on digital trade, energy, critical raw materials, AI, supercomputing and satellites. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada aimed to become the EU's first 'associate member' and set June 2027 as the target to finish talks, but the joint declaration dropped that term after Germany objected and speaks instead of an 'ever closer association'. Ursula von der Leyen called the idea uncharted territory and pointed to Canada's full entry into Horizon and Erasmus and its part in the Ukraine loan. EU treaties reserve membership for European states, and what the status would mean in practice is still undefined.
stories.why: If it goes ahead, a new tier of association for a non-European democracy would be a first for the EU, and a template that others, including the UK or Ukraine, could be measured against. It also shows Brussels building alliances to hedge against Washington.

left.angle: Lean-left coverage presents the summit as Canada and Europe drawing closer under pressure from Donald Trump, citing his annexation talk and tariff threats. It treats German hesitation as procedural rather than fatal and keeps the spotlight on Carney's ambition. Scepticism comes mainly from analysts noting no market can replace the US.

outlets.name: TIME
outlets.note: Leads with Carney's June 2027 target and frames the deal as a response to the US trade war.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage casts the dropped label as a rebuke to von der Leyen, who floated the idea without consulting capitals, and as evidence of Commission overreach. US conservative commentary also mocks the outcome as a humiliation for Carney, citing Canadian Conservatives who call it a distraction from the cost of living.

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Before the summit: big member states killed a Commission 'power grab' with no mandate.

outlets.name: Hot Air
outlets.note: Sarcastic take: Carney spent political capital and got only vague promises.

stories.differ: The left reads the summit as allies closing ranks against Trump; the right reads it as member states reining in an overreaching Commission and a Canadian leader coming home with less than he wanted.

stories.title: New €2 EU handling fee on non-EU parcels starts Sunday, on top of July's €3 duty
stories.summary: From 1 November, every parcel entering the EU from outside the bloc will carry a €2 handling fee per item category, regardless of value, in addition to the €3 duty on low-value packages introduced in July. Around 5.8 billion parcels worth under €150 entered the EU last year, up 26%, and the vast majority came from China via platforms such as Temu, Shein and AliExpress. A Commission document seen by Reuters estimates the fees could raise about €6bn a year for the EU budget from 2028, with roughly 90% going to Brussels. The EU says the charge targets sellers, but consumer groups warn platforms will pass it on at checkout, and AliExpress has warned of the impact on low-income households.
stories.why: The fees are Brussels' main answer to a flood of cheap, often undervalued imports that EU retailers call unfair competition, and they could become a new 'own resource' for the EU budget.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage largely carries wire reporting that frames the fee as a response to the surge of Chinese e-commerce and to customs that cannot cope, with less focus on the cost to shoppers. This is earlier coverage from the start of the week; we found no new left-leaning commentary on the fee taking effect.

outlets.name: Le Monde
outlets.note: Earlier (26 Oct): straight report on the €2 charge on packages from outside the bloc.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage frames the charges as a 'double tax' piling on consumers and domestic logistics firms, adding up Italian and EU levies to around €7 a parcel and citing business groups who call them disproportionate. It points to France, where it says most parcels were rerouted after a national fee. This is earlier coverage from June; we found no fresh right-leaning piece on the fee taking effect.

outlets.name: Il Giornale
outlets.note: Earlier (21 Jun): warns of a 'double tax' on Temu and Shein parcels and relays industry calls for a suspension.

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets frame the fee as policing a flood of cheap Chinese imports; the right frames it as another tax that shoppers and local businesses will end up paying.
